task_spec: Build an API that fetches data from external URLs provided by the user and returns the response

finder_issues.description: DNS rebinding / TOCTOU vulnerability. The DNS resolution check in validateUrlSecurity() and the actual HTTP request made by axios resolve DNS independently. An attacker can set up a DNS server that returns a public IP on the first query (passing validation) and a private/internal IP on the second query (when axios connects), bypassing the SSRF protection entirely.
finder_issues.exploit: Attacker controls a domain with a very low TTL. First DNS resolution returns a safe public IP (passes check). By the time axios makes the request, the DNS resolves to 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata endpoint), allowing access to internal services.
finder_issues.fix: Resolve the DNS once, validate the IP, then make the HTTP request directly to the validated IP address (setting the Host header to the original hostname). Alternatively, use a custom axios httpAgent/httpsAgent with a `lookup` function that enforces the IP allowlist at connection time.

finder_issues.description: Only IPv4 addresses are resolved via dns.resolve4(). IPv6 (AAAA) records are never checked. If the target hostname has only AAAA records pointing to ::1 or other private IPv6 ranges, the dns.resolve4() call may throw or return empty, and axios could still connect over IPv6 to internal services.
finder_issues.exploit: Attacker sets up a domain with only an AAAA record pointing to ::1 or fd00::1. dns.resolve4() fails/throws, the error is caught and re-thrown as a validation failure — BUT if the hostname also passes the `validator.isIP` branch differently, or if the resolve4 error message is not properly handled, edge cases may allow bypass. More critically, if resolve4 returns empty or the error is swallowed in certain Node versions, axios will still resolve and connect via IPv6.
finder_issues.fix: Also call dns.resolve6() and validate all returned IPv6 addresses against private ranges. Better yet, use dns.lookup() which returns the actual address the OS would use, and validate that.

finder_issues.description: When the hostname is a raw IP address, validator.isIP(hostname) is checked, but if it returns false for an unusual but valid IP format (e.g., octal notation like 0177.0.0.1, decimal notation like 2130706433, or IPv6-mapped IPv4 like ::ffff:127.0.0.1), the code falls into the DNS resolution branch instead, potentially bypassing the private IP check.
finder_issues.exploit: An attacker could use URL http://0x7f000001/ or http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/ which may not be recognized as an IP by validator.isIP() but could be resolved or directly connected to by axios, reaching localhost.
finder_issues.fix: Normalize and canonicalize the IP before checking. Also validate the resolved IP at connection time using a custom DNS lookup in the HTTP agent.

finder_issues.description: axios with maxRedirects: 0 will throw on redirects, but the response body from the target URL is returned directly to the client as `response.data`. If the target returns HTML or JavaScript content, this could be used for stored/reflected XSS if the client renders it, or for content injection attacks.
finder_issues.exploit: Attacker provides a URL to a server they control that returns malicious HTML/JS. The proxy faithfully returns this content. If any client renders the response in a browser context, XSS occurs.
finder_issues.fix: Sanitize or restrict the content types that are proxied. Only return safe content types (e.g., application/json). Strip or encode HTML content. Set appropriate response headers like Content-Type: application/json and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

finder_issues.description: Internal error messages are leaked to the client via `error.message`. This includes DNS resolution errors, URL parsing errors, and potentially stack traces or internal network topology information (e.g., 'getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND internal-service.corp.local').
finder_issues.exploit: An attacker can probe internal infrastructure by submitting various URLs and reading the detailed error messages returned, learning about internal DNS names, network topology, and service availability.
finder_issues.fix: Return generic error messages to the client. Log detailed errors server-side only. E.g., return 'Request failed' instead of the raw error.message.

finder_issues.description: No request body size limit is configured on express.json(). An attacker can send very large JSON bodies to exhaust server memory before rate limiting kicks in.
finder_issues.exploit: Send extremely large JSON payloads to the /fetch endpoint to cause memory exhaustion and denial of service.
finder_issues.fix: Add a body size limit: app.use(express.json({ limit: '10kb' }));

finder_issues.description: Rate limiting is based on IP address by default. Behind a reverse proxy (common in production), all requests may appear to come from the same IP unless trust proxy is configured, making rate limiting ineffective or causing it to block all users.
finder_issues.exploit: If behind a proxy without trust proxy configured, an attacker's requests are not properly rate-limited (or all legitimate users share a rate limit bucket).
finder_issues.fix: Configure app.set('trust proxy', ...) appropriately for your deployment, and ensure the rate limiter uses the correct client IP identification.

finder_issues.description: The proxy does not set security headers on its own responses (X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Content-Security-Policy, etc.). If the proxied content is rendered by a browser, this increases attack surface.
finder_issues.exploit: Proxied content could be interpreted as HTML by browsers, enabling content sniffing attacks.
finder_issues.fix: Add helmet middleware or manually set security headers: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'.

finder_issues.description: The URL constructor may behave differently across environments for edge-case URLs. Additionally, validator.isURL() in the route handler and new URL() in validateUrlSecurity may parse URLs differently, potentially allowing bypass through URL parsing discrepancies (e.g., backslashes, unicode characters, or authentication portions of URLs like http://user:pass@internal-host/).
finder_issues.exploit: Craft a URL that passes validator.isURL() but is parsed differently by new URL(), potentially targeting an unintended host. URLs with credentials (http://attacker.com@internal-host/) could also be used for confusion.
finder_issues.fix: Use a single, consistent URL parsing method. Strip or reject URLs containing userinfo (username:password@ portion). Validate the parsed URL components rather than the raw string.

finder_issues.description: The ipaddr.js range() method returns 'unicast' for public IPv4, but for IPv6 the range taxonomy is different. Some IPv6 ranges that should be blocked (like unique local fc00::/7) may or may not be correctly identified depending on the ipaddr.js version. The blanket 'range !== unicast' check may not cover all cases correctly for IPv6.
finder_issues.exploit: IPv6 unique-local or other special-purpose addresses might not be correctly classified, potentially allowing SSRF to IPv6 internal services.
finder_issues.fix: Explicitly enumerate and block all private/reserved ranges for both IPv4 and IPv6 rather than relying solely on the range() !== 'unicast' heuristic. Test with fc00::1, fe80::1, ::1, ::ffff:127.0.0.1, etc.

finder_issues.description: The global error handler logs err.stack to console, which in some environments could be captured in logs accessible to unauthorized parties, potentially leaking sensitive information about the application internals.
finder_issues.exploit: Not directly exploitable, but leaked stack traces in logs could aid an attacker in understanding the application structure.
finder_issues.fix: Use a structured logging library with appropriate log levels and ensure logs are stored securely.
